sentenceSets.sentence: The purist's objection to any adaptation of the method was taken seriously by those who had never tried to apply it outside the laboratory.

answerChoices.reasoning: A traditionalist honors inherited practice broadly, but the objection here is narrowly to altering one specific method in any respect.
A skeptic doubts the method works at all, whereas this complaint is about changing it, which takes for granted that the original form is sound.
A theorist is occupied with why the method works, while the recorded grievance concerns departures from how it was originally laid down.
A pedant quibbles over trivia, yet the objection covers adaptation of the method as a whole and is described as taken seriously.
A veteran would have long field experience, but the sentence contrasts this figure's audience with people who have actually applied the method outside the lab.
The inventor would be the method's author, and nothing identifies this objector as the person who devised it.
A gatekeeper controls who is admitted, while this objection concerns how the method itself may be used.
A critic attacks the method, but this figure is defending it against alteration.
An innovator would welcome the very adaptations being objected to.
Judging by what works in practice is what the sentence assigns to those who use the method outside the laboratory.
A dabbler would not raise an objection anyone took seriously.

sentenceSets.sentence: Some purists still insist that the word cannot be used that way, though the usage has been in print for two hundred years.

answerChoices.reasoning: A grammarian sets out how a language actually behaves, and two centuries of printed use is exactly the evidence such a person would credit rather than dismiss.
Lexicographers record the uses that exist, which the sentence says have been amply attested in print, yet these people refuse to acknowledge them.
Political allegiance is not at issue; what is insisted on is the proper handling of a single word.
A scold rebukes people for their behavior, but the claim reported here is about what the word itself can mean.
Editors work over particular manuscripts, while the usage in question has been passing through print for two centuries.
Etymology traces where a word came from, whereas the argument here concerns whether a present-day use is allowed.
Poets stretch usage rather than forbid it.
Commentators hold forth on public affairs, and this dispute is confined to the propriety of one word.
Iconoclasts attack received rules, the opposite of insisting on one.
Libertines throw off restraint, while these people are imposing it.
Someone unable to read would not be arguing about two hundred years of printed usage.

sentenceSets.sentence: A purist would tell you the sauce takes four hours and a copper pan; the restaurant makes it in forty minutes and nobody has complained.

answerChoices.reasoning: A connoisseur judges quality wherever it turns up, but this figure prescribes a procedure — four hours, a particular pan — and the diners are perfectly satisfied without it.
A gourmand loves eating, whereas the person here is laying down how the sauce must be made.
A perfectionist wants the best result, yet nobody has complained about the result, so what is being defended is the method itself.
A craftsman makes the thing with his own hands, while this person is telling you what the making supposedly requires.
The restaurant's cooks are the ones actually turning the sauce out in forty minutes.
A sommelier's province is wine, not how long a sauce should simmer.
Gluttony concerns how much is eaten, not how the sauce is prepared.
Someone still learning the method would not be pronouncing on what it demands.
A philistine has no interest in such refinements at all.
A hack turns work out carelessly and would never insist on four hours and a copper pan.
The customers are the ones not complaining, so they are not the source of the objection.
